title: Opposition: The Work Is Stopped
summary: The peoples settled around Judah offer to help build the temple, claiming to worship the same God, but Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse. Those peoples then discourage and frighten the builders and hire counselors against them through the reign of Cyrus and into that of Darius. The chapter then looks ahead to later accusations under Xerxes and Artaxerxes, including a letter that persuades Artaxerxes to halt the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, before returning to note that work on the temple stopped until the second year of Darius.
story: Chapter 3 ended with a foundation laid and a sound of joy and weeping heard far away. Chapter 4 shows who heard it. From here on, every stage of the restoration in Ezra and Nehemiah meets resistance, and this chapter sets out the pattern. It begins with an offer that sounds generous, moves to open discouragement and bribery, and ends with a royal decree that stops the work by force. The writer steps outside strict time order to gather several episodes of opposition, spanning about ninety years, into one account. The effect is to show that the struggle was not a passing setback but the ongoing condition of the returned community. The final verse brings the reader back to the temple and the reign of Darius, where chapter 5 resumes the story.
historical:
The people who approach Zerubbabel say they were brought to the land by Esarhaddon, king of Assyria (681-669 BC). Assyria had deported the population of the northern kingdom after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and settled people from other lands in its place (2 Kings 17:24-41), and this verse suggests further settlements under Esarhaddon. Second Kings describes those settlers as fearing the LORD while also serving their own gods. Ashurbanipal, named in verse 10 (the Assyrian king who reigned about 669 to 631 BC), is credited with more deportations. These groups, in and around Samaria, are the ancestors of the people later known as Samaritans, though the full split between Jews and Samaritans came later.

Verses 6 to 23 jump forward in time. Verse 5 has already mentioned Darius I (522-486 BC). Verse 6 moves to Xerxes (486-465 BC), and verses 7 to 23 to Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC). The letter of Rehum and Shimshai concerns not the temple, which was finished in 515 BC, but the city walls, and Artaxerxes' order to stop that work is probably the background to the ruined walls Nehemiah hears about in 445 BC (Nehemiah 1:3). Verse 24 then returns to the time of Darius, when work on the temple had stopped, and picks up the thread for chapter 5.
cultural:
Temple building in the ancient world was a political act. A rebuilt temple gave a community a center, a treasury, and a claim on the land. For the returned exiles, sharing the work with people whose worship mixed the LORD with other gods would have meant sharing the identity of the community itself, and they refused. Their appeal to Cyrus's decree is also a legal point: the permission had been granted to them. Their neighbors, for their part, had lived on the land for generations and may have seen the returnees as newcomers claiming authority over a region that was not theirs.

The Persian empire ran on written reports and royal archives, and verses 8-22 show that system at work. Officials in the province write to the king, warn that Jerusalem has a history of rebellion, and point out that a fortified city might withhold tribute, duty, and toll, the taxes that fed the royal treasury. The king has the records searched, finds that Jerusalem did rebel against Assyria and Babylon, and orders the work to stop. The officials' argument is shrewd: they appeal not to religion but to the king's revenue and security.
literary: At verse 8 the language of the book changes from Hebrew to Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, and stays in Aramaic until 6:18. Verse 7 even notes that the letter was written in Aramaic. The chapter is arranged by theme rather than date: first a summary of opposition under Cyrus and Darius (verses 1-5), then a quick note about Xerxes (verse 6), then a long quotation of the correspondence under Artaxerxes (verses 7-23), and finally a verse that resumes the main story (verse 24). The repetition of verse 5's reference to Darius in verse 24 frames the flash-forward, a technique ancient writers used to show a pattern. The letters themselves follow standard Persian official form, with senders, recipients, greeting, and a formula such as let it be known to the king.

outline.t: The people of the land discourage the builders
The letter to Artaxerxes against Jerusalem
The king's reply halts the rebuilding of the city
The temple work stands still until Darius's second year

doctrines.note: The refusal in verse 3 rests on the conviction that the LORD's house must be built by those committed to him alone. Holiness in the Old Testament means belonging wholly to God, and the returnees feared that sharing the work with those who also served other gods would compromise it.

The builders face fear, discouragement, bribery, and finally forced stoppage. The chapter does not explain why God allows the delay; it records it honestly, teaching that faithful work may suffer long interruption without God having abandoned it.

The same Persian archives that are used to stop the work here will be used in chapters 5 and 6 to restart it. The chapter shows the machinery of empire turning against God's people, but the book as a whole shows that machinery under God's hand.

words.note: Sitnah, accusation, from the same root as satan, meaning adversary or accuser. In verse 6 it names the formal charge lodged against the people of Judah under Xerxes. The word pictures opposition that works through legal complaint, the kind of hostility the rest of the chapter documents.

Betel, an Aramaic verb meaning to cease or stop, used four times at the chapter's end. The king orders the builders to stop, they are forcibly stopped, and the temple work ceases. The repetition makes the stoppage feel heavy and final, which sets up the surprise of chapter 5.

Merad, rebellion, used in the king's reply (verse 19). The accusation that Jerusalem was a rebellious city was not false: Judah had rebelled against both Assyria and Babylon. The enemies use Judah's real history against it, a reminder that the returnees carried their past with them.

christ: The chapter's refusal to share the work with those who worshiped other gods alongside the LORD belongs to a period when Israel's survival as a distinct people was at stake. The New Testament tells a later part of the story in which the descendants of those northern settlers, the Samaritans, are drawn into the people of God. Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman about worship not in this mountain or in Jerusalem but in spirit and truth (John 4:19-24), makes a Samaritan the hero of a parable, and sends his disciples to Judea and Samaria (Acts 1:8). That is not a correction of Ezra so much as the next chapter of the same story: the concern for true worship remains, while the boundary of God's people is redrawn around Jesus. The chapter's portrait of a righteous work opposed by false accusation also matches a pattern the Gospels trace in Jesus' own trial, where charges of rebellion were brought before a Roman governor.

hard.q: Were Zerubbabel and Jeshua right to refuse the help of people who said they worshiped the same God?
hard.a:
The refusal can look narrow to a modern reader. The people who offered help said they sought the same God and had sacrificed to him for generations, and their later hostility could be read as a reaction to being rejected. On the other hand, 2 Kings 17:33 describes these settlers as fearing the LORD while serving their own gods, and the book presents their offer as coming from adversaries whose later actions reveal their intent. The returnees' concern was not ethnic purity as such but the integrity of worship: a temple shared with a mixed religion would no longer be the house of the LORD alone.

Interpreters differ in emphasis. Some read the chapter as a necessary act of faithfulness at a fragile moment, when the community could easily have been absorbed. Others note that the prophets of the period, and later the New Testament, looked for a day when the nations would join in worship of the LORD, and they see the chapter as reflecting a particular stage in God's purposes rather than a permanent rule. Most agree that the text itself approves the refusal and grounds it in Cyrus's decree and the exclusive worship of the LORD.

questions: The offer of help in verse 2 sounded generous. How can a community tell the difference between genuine partnership and help that would change who it is?
The enemies used Jerusalem's real history of rebellion against it. How do you respond when your past failures are used to discourage you from doing something good now?
The work stood still for years. What sustains faithfulness in a season when good work has been stopped and nothing seems to move?
